2.name: Acid Arrow
2.mathfinder_summary: This was considered very good for damage, especially for Maguses, but has since been replaced by Acid Grip which many overlook due to nostalgia for this spell. As an attack roll spell, you'll benefit from teamwork buffs and Sure Strike more than save-based alternatives, making it better for confirmed kills when you can stack bonuses. However, the baseline math is worse since you lack potency runes, and with no partial effects on a miss, accuracy becomes crucial. Against bosses, expect success (~50% hit rate) as your baseline outcome rather than crits.

865.name: Ash Cloud
865.mathfinder_summary: Excellent boss control spell that zones enemies away while dealing persistent fire damage and potentially blinding them. Use this for area denial and pyromancer variety, especially against single powerful foes you want to reposition. The Fortitude save gives you a hidden advantage since most AoE spells target Reflex, and many monsters have weaker Fort saves. The persistent damage and blind rider effects add massive value beyond raw damage numbers. Note that Wrath Runelords can block this with their "can't create" anathema, limiting its utility in that specific campaign.

1350.name: Cinder Swarm
1350.mathfinder_summary: Excellent multimodal sustained damage spell that replaces Floating Flame at rank 4. Use fireflies mode for crowd control and fire ants mode for single-target focus fire. The forced movement rider can completely nullify grab-based threats by pulling enemies away each turn. Consider the incapacitation variant situationally for AoE blinding against groups. Stays relevant through high levels due to strong scaling and ally-friendly targeting.

1422.name: Elemental Sense
1422.mathfinder_summary: At high level, daily-cast this from a spare high-rank slot to scout - it reveals nearby elemental presence, even through walls, and the long duration makes it efficient once your low slots run surplus. Its value is campaign-dependent: handy when the GM hides elemental threats or you need to read what's past a barrier, wasted otherwise. Like most utility it solves its problem outright with no check, and a spare-slot daily cast costs almost nothing in combat prowess. Carry it when scouting and detection regularly matter at your table.

1423.name: Summon Elemental Herald
1423.mathfinder_summary: This incarnate spell delivers massive value from a single 8th-rank slot through its arrival and departure mechanics, giving you all three actions free on the departure turn. The elemental herald likely offers reliable damage output that can bypass traditional defenses, making it effective against high-AC or high-save enemies where other spells might struggle. Use this when you need sustained battlefield presence and can capitalize on both the initial summoning impact and the guaranteed departure effect.

Against multiple targets, focus on the high probability that someone will fail rather than average damage - the failure effects become your primary planning tool, especially since critical failures become increasingly likely against weaker foes.

As a Fortitude-targeting attack roll spell, it benefits from the hidden advantage that many monsters have weaker Fort saves compared to Reflex, plus it synergizes well with Sure Strike, hero points, and ally buffs for confirmed kills. However, the lack of partial effects means misses hurt more than save spells, and you'll fall 1-3 behind martials in attack bonus without potency runes. Best used situationally when you can stack attack bonuses or need guaranteed barrier removal rather than as your primary damage option.

1503.name: Dream Message
1503.mathfinder_summary: Contact someone at the other end of the world with no skill equivalent - this spell just works without any checks. As a utility spell, its value is highly campaign-dependent; long-distance communication becomes invaluable in campaigns with separated parties or distant NPCs, but useless if your adventures stay local. At rank 3, the spell slot cost is moderate, making it worthwhile when mundane communication methods fail. Consider preparing this when you expect to need reliable long-range messaging that can't be intercepted or blocked by normal means.

1508.name: Eclipse Burst
1508.mathfinder_summary: This is the premier rank 7 AoE blast, dealing 18d6 damage that outscales heightened Fireball and becomes the new damage benchmark. The critical failure blindness effect is devastating - against 6 enemies you have a 62% chance of permanently blinding at least one, essentially removing them from combat. Even without critical failures, the raw damage is excellent with low opportunity cost. However, it can hit allies, so positioning matters. The combination of top-tier damage with a potentially fight-ending rider effect makes this a signature-worthy spell for blaster builds.

1515.name: Entangling Flora
1515.mathfinder_summary: Already a strong spell for slowing and immobilizing enemies, this lingering area control generates value over time after casting. The automatic difficult terrain provides unconditional reliability, while against multiple targets someone will likely fail their save for the immobilization effect. Use positioning and scouting to maximize value by forcing enemies into divide-and-conquer choices. Combos well with forced movement effects like Acid Grip - push enemies back into the zone after they've saved and started approaching. The success effect looks weak individually but creates meaningful tactical complications across multiple foes.

1533.name: Floating Flame

Gets outclassed by Cinder Swarm at higher ranks but remains solid when cast one rank below maximum.

1538.name: Freeze Time
1538.mathfinder_summary: This is objectively one of the most powerful 10th rank spells available, giving you complete battlefield control by stopping time for everyone except yourself. As a utility spell with automatic effects and no saving throw, it provides unconditional reliability that's extremely rare at any spell rank. Use this when you need to reposition the entire party, set up devastating combos, or escape impossible situations. The campaign-dependent nature of utility spells means its value varies, but the sheer power of manipulating time itself makes it universally impactful when the situation calls for it.

1541.name: Gecko Grip
1541.mathfinder_summary: Keep a scroll for time-pressured climbs - at once-per-adventure frequency it doesn't merit a wand, but cheap scroll insurance is well worth it. The spell erases Athletics checks for climbing, which matters most early when your bonus is modest. As you advance, high-Athletics characters gain quick-climb abilities or natural climb speeds that outpace this rank 2 fix, so lean on it early and expect to replace it later. A spare low-rank slot or a scroll makes carrying it nearly free when you need to scale something fast.

1542.name: Gentle Landing
1542.mathfinder_summary: Mathfinder considers this great utility that solves fall damage problems outright without requiring checks. As a reaction spell, it provides excellent action economy by activating on others' turns while costing minimal resources from your low-rank slots. The cheap slot cost makes it particularly valuable for filling lower-level spell slots at higher levels, and spontaneous casters can always have it ready when needed. Use this when your campaign involves significant vertical terrain, flying enemies, or forced movement effects that could cause fall damage to you or allies.

1555.name: Heroism
1555.mathfinder_summary: A strong buff with duration that largely replaces Bless at rank 5 and should be heightened past that point. As a single-target spell, prioritize it for its success effect since bosses will succeed roughly 50% of the time against your spell DC. The +1 status bonus to attack rolls, perception checks, saves, and skill checks provides reliable value even when enemies resist the fear immunity portion. Divine casters can fit this into support builds alongside their naturally hard-to-resist damage types, while Occult casters benefit from its Will save targeting that complements their natural strengths.

1561.name: Hydraulic Push
1561.mathfinder_summary: A good spell with strong utility beyond damage - the push effect bypasses normal forced movement restrictions, letting you shove enemies off ledges or into hazardous terrain. While it's an attack roll spell that lacks the potency runes martials enjoy, it benefits from teamwork buffs and hero points for confirmed kills. The push rider makes this inherently stronger than other forced movement options. Consider it as one signature attack spell option rather than loading up on multiple attack roll spells, and remember it competes with other solid rank 1 blasts like Horizon Thunder Sphere.

1564.name: Hypnotize
1564.mathfinder_summary: One of the most criminally underrated spells in the game. The real value isn't the Fascinated condition—it's the automatic Dazzled on all creatures in the area with no save, creating a lose-lose situation where enemies either accept a 20% miss chance or waste an action leaving the area. As a sustained spell, you get excellent action economy by casting it turn one then sustaining for one action while using your remaining two actions for focus spells or other offense. The zone control combines well with prone/immobilize effects from allies to create devastating action-denial stacks.

1569.name: Illusory Object
1569.mathfinder_summary: This classic multimodal spell offers huge versatility in one rank 1 slot - wall off battlefield sections, trap enemies who must disbelieve to pass through, protect ally flanks, divide and conquer, or simply create barriers to escape behind. As a utility spell, it solves problems outright without checks in most cases, making it especially valuable at low levels when spell slots are expensive but can outperform skills. The illusion's effectiveness depends heavily on campaign context and enemy types, but its tactical applications for battlefield control make it a strong consideration for any arcane or occult caster's repertoire.

1572.mathfinder_summary: Very powerful single-target blast that's rarely worth using your 10th-rank slot on—signature it at rank 9 as a formality instead. Best for longer combats where you can extract maximum value from the sustained effect over multiple rounds.

1581.name: Knock
1581.mathfinder_summary: The poster child of the 'Knock Problem': a +4 status bonus to Thievery that allows untrained attempts but still demands a check, so a strong enough lock can beat the counteract - unlike D&D's auto-success. Even so, surplus low-rank slots make carrying it affordable, and it can outperform skills at low levels when a slot is precious but impactful. Use it when your party lacks reliable lockpicking or faces tough locks; just don't expect a guaranteed open. Utility value rides on how often your campaign puts locked doors in your way.

1586.name: Lightning Bolt
1586.mathfinder_summary: Treat this as a single-target spell with a multi-target rider rather than a true AoE - the line shape typically hits only 2-3 enemies. It matches Thunder Strike's single-target damage but becomes incredibly efficient when hitting exactly 2 targets in narrow corridors. Consider it over Fireball for prepared casters since it works both single-target and multi-target, making it more versatile for spell slot economy. Particularly valuable when going late in initiative for kill confirms due to higher single-target damage while potentially catching additional enemies.

1589.name: Lock
1589.mathfinder_summary: This is the counterpart to Knock, setting a lock's DC to your spellcasting DC or the existing DC, whichever is higher. Like most utility spells, it solves problems outright without requiring checks, making it campaign-dependent in value. At low levels, spending a spell slot for utility is expensive but can outperform skills, while at high levels the same low-rank slot becomes cheap though skills may have caught up. Use this to secure areas when you need reliable protection that scales with your magical prowess rather than relying on mundane locks.

1592.mathfinder_summary: This is objectively one of the most powerful 10th rank spells available, offering incredible utility that can solve problems outright without requiring checks. Consider whether your campaign presents problems that justify using your single 10th-level slot on utility rather than combat power.

1611.name: Mystic Armor
1611.mathfinder_summary: Massively underrated spell that's fantastic at rank 10 due to enormous gold savings (equivalent to 7-9 scrolls worth of value), making it better than most combat options at that level. At rank 1, it's pretty good if you lack armor proficiency, bringing you within 1 AC of medium armor instead of 2. The middle levels (5-14) are a toss-up—decent if you have plans for the saved gold, but weakest at levels 15-18 where gold savings are minimal. Consider retraining into it at high levels even if you never used it before, as the economic value outweighs most alternatives in slow-to-medium attrition campaigns.

1737.name: Vanishing Tracks
1737.mathfinder_summary: Covers tracks with +4 DC or your spellcasting DC, but remains check-based since skilled trackers can counter magic. 1742.name: Vision of Death
1742.mathfinder_summary: Criminally underrated single-target debuff+damage hybrid that's competitive with Synesthesia when all factors are weighed. Delivers mini-fireball damage while inflicting frightened, making it excellent against bosses where the success effect matters most. Strong Will-targeting option that belongs on every debuffer's list with access. Note that prepared casters can flexibly swap it in when party synergies (like Dirge of Doom) make frightened less redundant. Check your GM's interpretation of death immunity—RAW only blocks instant-kill, not the mental damage or frightened condition.

1755.name: Water Breathing
1755.mathfinder_summary: The poster child for scroll insurance - buy it as a scroll, since you'll want it about once per adventure, it covers the whole party all day, and it costs trivial gold. Weigh your campaign's odds of underwater encounters, then keep a scroll in your pocket.

2025.name: Shared Invisibility
2025.mathfinder_summary: Makes the whole party invisible, solving stealth challenges outright without checks. As a utility spell, its value is highly campaign-dependent - excellent for infiltration-heavy games but situational otherwise. The emanation area is significantly larger than equivalent bursts and naturally excludes enemies, making positioning easier. At rank 3, this represents good value since utility spells become relatively cheaper at higher levels while skills catch up to lower-rank effects. Best used when you need guaranteed group stealth rather than individual invisibility options.

335.name: Telepathic Bond
335.mathfinder_summary: Use this for all-day party telepathy - coordination that's always nice to have. Wand it for daily use, or once your high-level slots run surplus, daily-cast it from a spare 5th-rank slot. It's Uncommon, so buying a wand or scroll needs GM access. The opportunity cost is low: party-wide telepathy costs only gold or a spare slot, never combat prowess. Worth carrying whenever your group splits up, scouts ahead, or needs silent coordination - which in most campaigns is often.

observations.source: How to Blast GOOD in Pathfinder 2e.md
observations.observation: Against three targets at on-level DCs, there is an ~83% chance at least one target fails the save. The 'three successes' outcome is about half as likely as 'two fails, one success'.

observations.source: How to Blast GOOD in Pathfinder 2e.md
observations.observation: AoE creates focus fire opportunities. The spike damage on a failed save brings one target into kill range; allies finish that target while the caster continues softening the rest.

observations.observation: Evaluate debuffs by outcomes changed, not raw numbers. A -1 to AC that converts a miss to a hit or a hit to a crit is worth one 'outcome changed.'

observations.source: Pathfinder 2e Spellcaster MYTHS - ALWAYS Assume Enemies Will Succeed.md

observations.observation: One-action sustained damage is premium action economy. Getting cantrip-level damage for a single action on subsequent turns frees two actions for focus spells, slotted spells, or cantrips each turn.

1631.name: Phantasmal Minion
1631.mathfinder_summary: Treat this as always-on telekinesis - a cheap scroll or wand for fetch-and-carry chores and hands-free tasks out of combat. It summons an effect, not a combatant with its own HP and actions, so its value is pure utility, not battlefield control. Buy it as a consumable for occasional needs or wand it if your table leans on it daily; either way it costs no combat prowess. How often it earns its keep depends on your campaign's exploration and problem-solving demands.

observations.observation: At low levels, using a spell slot for utility is expensive but can outperform skills. At high levels, that same low-rank slot is cheap but skills have caught up or surpassed it.

observations.source: Are Utility Spells BAD in Pathfinder 2e.md
observations.observation: Spells that contest a foe's skill involve a check because the world has adapted to magic, creating stable worldbuilding where non-magical skill remains relevant.

observations.source: How to Look at Spells on Archives of Nethys.md
observations.observation: Arcane is privileged — it can target all four defenses at all levels with a full variety of spells. Most other traditions can do two saves + AC but struggle with the third.

observations.source: Who are the BEST Blasters in Pathfinder 2e.md
observations.observation: The gold standard for blasting fundamentals — best defense targeting, best brute forcing, best damage variety, best riders, best low-rank value.

observations.source: Who are the BEST Blasters in Pathfinder 2e.md
observations.observation: Naturally good at targeting Will saves and can cover Reflex and Fortitude gaps when combined with granted spells.

observations.source: Witch and Wizard Blaster Build Guides.md
observations.observation: Arcane is the better blasting tradition than Primal for two reasons: Will-targeting blasts become available from rank 3 onward, whereas Primal's Will-targeting options lean debuff rather than blast, and Shore Strike and Force Barrage provide a reliability floor that Primal lacks entirely.

observations.source: Theoretical vs Practical Utility Spells.md
observations.observation: Buying heuristic: scroll for once-per-adventure needs, wand for once-per-day needs. Consumable utility costs zero combat prowess.

observations.source: Theoretical vs Practical Utility Spells.md
observations.observation: Past ~level 7, surplus low-rank slots make slot-cast utility nearly free - skipping it leaves power on the table.

observations.source: Theoretical vs Practical Utility Spells.md
observations.observation: PF2e utility is weaker spell-for-spell than D&D's but sees more table play - opportunity cost, not raw power, drives actual usage.

observations.observation: Don't need success effects at all since if the spell whiffs, you still have most of your turn. Fishing for failures is valid when action cost is low.
